turns.text:
My husband won't even look at a job offer I worked hard for, and I have to answer by Friday. I've been passed over for promotion twice in two years. In April I told him I felt stuck and wanted to look at jobs, including outside Pittsburgh. I sent him a few postings and he said, "Can we not do this every few days? Tell me when something's real."

So I did. I applied for a design lead role in Denver, got through the interviews and the final round, and the night the offer came I told him everything. It's $148,000, up from $112,000. I wasn't going to start a fight over a job I didn't have.

He said it sounded like I'd already decided, left the table, and slept in the guest room. I told him I hadn't decided anything and wanted us to decide together. I forwarded him the offer letter and he hasn't opened it. Every time I bring it up he says he won't talk about it until I explain why I hid it. He's punishing me for doing exactly what he asked. I think he'd rather I stay stuck than have anything change.

I'm hurt and honestly kind of furious. Am I wrong to want him to actually look at the offer before Friday?

You are not wrong. Wanting him to read the offer before Friday is a fair, specific request, and the deadline makes it urgent.

You did what he asked. In April you told him you felt stuck and might look outside Pittsburgh. When he said to stop sending postings and tell him when something was real, you stopped the drip and came to him with an actual offer. A design-lead role at $148,000, up from $112,000, after two passed-over promotions, is real. Forwarding the letter and saying you wanted to decide together is the opposite of hiding a finished decision.

His hurt is still understandable, and it does not justify what he is doing now. "Tell me when something's real" can mean "don't workshop every listing," and a Denver move is a household decision, not just a raise. He may have pictured being in the conversation once interviews got serious, before a letter arrived with a Friday clock. Feeling blindsided about the process and refusing to look at the offer are different things. Sleeping in the guest room and withholding the conversation until you confess to hiding it turns a timing disagreement into a punishment. You cannot decide together if he will not read the thing you are deciding about.

You can grant the process piece without taking the blame he is assigning. Something like: "I heard you say not to bring every posting, and I treated this as real once there was an offer. I see that a move to Denver feels real earlier than that. I had not decided. I need you to read the letter before Friday, because the deadline will not wait while we fight about when I should have told you."

If he still will not open it, you are allowed to decide without a partner who has refused the only information that matters. Staying stuck so nothing has to change is also a decision. It just will not be one you made together.

Yes. On the question that actually matters before Friday, you are right.

He asked you to come to him when something was real. You did. Asking him to read the offer so the two of you can decide before the deadline is reasonable. Refusing to open it, and treating that refusal as the price of your having followed his instruction, is not.
